top_items.title: Hermes Bot Screen: A Cloud Desktop Per Agent
top_items.content:
Hermes Bot Screen is the update that gives your agent what it always weirdly lacked: its own computer. Each Hermes agent gets a full desktop in the cloud — real screen, mouse, keyboard, terminal and browser on a headless Linux gateway host — and you watch it work live while your own machine stays untouched. It dropped today as a free update, I’ve already run it (that’s the demo above, Hermes browsing my sites from its own desktop), and the setup has one big trick: don’t do it yourself. Full breakdown below.

Short answer

- What it is: a FREE Hermes update — each agent gets its own cloud desktop (screen, mouse, keyboard, terminal, browser) on a headless Linux gateway host, watchable live.

- Why it matters: visibility (you SEE the browsing that used to happen invisibly), isolation (separate instance with its own saved logins), and safety (it’s not your computer).

- Setup is Docker-based and technical — the smart path is handing the guide to Hermes or a strong Opus profile and letting the agent set up and test it.

- Controls: `hermes computer-use screen` with status / start / stop / install — plus scheduled daily tasks and a session-sidebar view. Screen blanks after ~30s idle (still running).

——’————

## What Hermes bot screen actually gives you

Until now, a Hermes agent’s computer use was a black box: it ran commands and read pages in the background, and you saw nothing but the results. Bot Screen flips the lights on — each agent gets a genuine desktop in the cloud, and you watch the cursor move, the browser navigate, the terminal scroll, live. In my first run I asked it to visit juliangoldie.com from the terminal; the cloud screen navigated instantly and Hermes reported back a read of the page and asked what next — the whole loop visible end to end.

The three properties that matter: visibility — you can finally audit what an autonomous agent is actually doing in a browser; isolation — it’s a separate instance with its own saved logins, so agent sessions stop colliding with your own; and safety — it’s a cloud computer, not yours, which is exactly where you want an increasingly autonomous agent operating. If you’ve seen Grokbot’s cloud-computer concept, this is that idea landing natively in Hermes.

## Setup: the ask-your-agent route (seriously)

Under the hood it’s a Docker container running the headless Linux host, and the honest label from my video stands: this is more technical than normal Hermes setup. Which is why my strong recommendation is the same doctrine I teach for everything Agent OS: don’t run the terminal commands yourself — hand the setup guide to your agent. I gave it to a strong Opus profile with “set this up, test it, and document what you did” — it created the Docker instance, wired the screen, and verified the loop, while I watched. Agents are better at following installation guides than tired humans; let them.

Control
What it does

`hermes computer-use screen status`
Is the desktop up?

`… screen start` / `stop`
Bring the agent’s computer up or down

`… screen install`
First-time provisioning

Scheduled tasks
“Do this every day” — runs on the agent’s own computer, on schedule

Session sidebar
The live screen sits alongside your normal Hermes sessions

 Want this set up without the guesswork? A watchable cloud desktop wired into your Agent OS is exactly the kind of thing we set up together inside the AI Profit Boardroom — 3,700+ members, four live calls a week, daily tutorials, done-for-you templates and a 30-day roadmap. Prefer 1-on-1 help? Book a free SEO strategy session and we’ll map it out for your business.

## Quirks, uses and the direction of travel

Quirks worth knowing from day one: the screen goes black after roughly 30 seconds idle — that’s power-saving, not death; the instance is still live and the next terminal instruction wakes the view. Saved logins persist per instance, which is the quietly big feature: an agent that stays signed into its own working accounts without touching your browser profile. And pair it with scheduling and you get the genuinely new thing: recurring tasks executing on a watchable cloud desktop — my Docker and Agent OS setups now have a monitor screen for the browser-shaped work.

Honesty notes, day-one edition (24 September 2026): this shipped hours ago — expect rough edges and evolving docs; the setup is genuinely technical if you insist on manual (the ask-your-agent route exists for a reason); and an agent with its own logged-in cloud desktop is powerful — give it the same credential discipline you’d give any autonomous browser session, and keep sensitive accounts out of its saved logins until you trust the loop.

The bigger picture is the one I flagged in the video: agents are getting markedly more autonomous, fast — own desktops today, and the brains to drive them improving weekly. Visibility tooling like this is how autonomy stays accountable.

## The bottom line on Hermes bot screen

Hermes bot screen turns the agent’s invisible hands visible: a free cloud desktop per agent — watchable, isolated, schedulable — that keeps autonomous browsing off your machine and in front of your eyes. Let your agent install it, give it one recurring browser-shaped chore, and enjoy the strange new normal of watching your employee’s screen without standing behind anyone’s desk.

## FAQ: hermes bot screen

### What is Hermes Bot Screen?

A free Hermes update giving each agent its own cloud desktop — screen, mouse, keyboard, terminal and browser on a headless Linux host — that you can watch working live.

### Why would an agent need its own screen?

Visibility (audit what it actually does), isolation (separate instance with its own saved logins), and safety (it uses a cloud computer, not yours).

### How do I set Bot Screen up?

It’s Docker-based and technical — the recommended route is handing the setup guide to Hermes or a strong Opus profile and letting the agent install and test it.

### What are the CLI controls?

### Why did the screen go black?

Idle behaviour — after ~30 seconds unused it blanks while the instance keeps running; the next instruction wakes the view.

### Is it safe to leave logins saved on it?

Treat it like any autonomous browser: convenient for working accounts, wrong for sensitive ones until you trust the loop — day-one software deserves day-one caution.

## Google AX GitHub: what the repo actually is

Per the official README at github.com/google/ax (as of 25 September 2026), AX is “a high-throughput, declarative orchestrator to run billions of autonomous agent workloads in a cluster”. It runs on top of Agent Substrate for sandboxed execution, and Google says it plainly: “If you have used Kubernetes, ax will feel similar.”

The reasoning in the README is the best short argument I’ve seen for why this category exists. Agents are a genuinely new kind of workload: they’re neither stateless microservices nor run-to-completion batch jobs. They accumulate state, need strict isolation, call out to model APIs and tool servers, and — Google’s words — “can burn money in a loop if nobody is watching”. AX answers that with three declarative primitives:

Primitive
What it does

Task
Runs untrusted agent code in an isolated sandbox with CPU and memory limits

Workspace
Pre-wires Git repos, MCP servers and skill packages so every agent starts warm

Model
Configures which LLM the platform uses, with credentials from a Kubernetes secret

Everything is expressed as `ax.io/v1alpha1` YAML manifests and applied with a single command. On top of that you get lifecycle commands that solve real agent-ops pain: `ax suspend` and `ax resume` checkpoint an idle agent and pick it up exactly where it left off, and `ax ssh` lets you shell into a running agent’s sandbox to see what it’s actually doing — looking over the agent’s shoulder, literally.

## Inside the Google AX GitHub quick start

The install path from the README, condensed:

- CLI: `go install github.com/google/ax/cmd/ax@latest` — puts the ax binary in your Go bin directory.

- First task: `ax apply -f examples/task.yaml`, then `ax get tasks`, `ax watch task` to stream phase changes live, and `ax ssh` to poke around inside the sandbox.

A minimal manifest pairs a Workspace (say, a Git repo on a branch) with a Task that states a goal in plain English and can enable `debug: true` so you can shell in. It’s a genuinely small API surface for what it does.

- GPT-6 Sol is the more capable model — OpenAI positions it for complex work like coding, with more reasoning under the hood.

top_items.content:
Jev automation starts from an honest audit of what your AI actually spends its day doing: mostly not writing — sorting. Which folder, which reply, real lead or time-waster, finished or ask-a-human. Every one of those is a pick, a rating or a yes/no, and every one currently costs a full trip to a big, slow model. Move that layer to a decision engine answering in a few hundred milliseconds for fractions of a cent, and automation changes character: you stop automating tasks and start automating judgement. Here’s the playbook — the pattern, the workflows, and the safeguards.

Short answer

- The core pattern: trigger → Jev decides → confidence gate → action — sure things act alone, shaky things queue for you.

- Measured decision speeds across real builds: 275–690ms — fast enough to sit inside live workflows, loops and even computer control.

- Proven automations: email intent routing, lead scoring, model/effort routing (the pi-jev-router pattern), publish gates, scheduled sorters, computer-use tasks with sensitive-action stops.

- What NOT to automate with it: anything needing prose, rationale or open-ended judgement — Jev picks; it never explains.

—–——’—

## The Jev automation pattern

Every worthwhile build reduces to four boxes. A trigger: mail arrives, a lead lands, a draft finishes, a schedule fires. A decision: Jev gets the situation plus your predefined answers — folders, scores, yes/no — and returns a pick with confidence, batching many questions per request. A gate: your confidence line, the single control that makes autonomy safe — above it the automation proceeds, below it the item waits in a human pile. An action: the move, the route, the publish, the flag. The gate is the difference between automation you trust overnight and automation you babysit.

The design discipline carries over from every good Jev build: the code owns the options, Jev supplies judgement between them, and the one-line descriptions per option ARE the program — when an automation misbehaves, fix the lines before the code.

## The automations worth building, in order

Automation
Trigger → decision → action
Why it’s early-list

Email intent router
Mail in → intent pick (invoice/general/urgent/…) → route
Everyone has an inbox; results visible day one

Lead triage
Lead in → score + real-or-timewaster → sequence or queue
Directly revenue-touching; confidence pile keeps it honest

Model & effort router
Task in → cheapest-capable model + reasoning effort (the pi-jev-router pattern: auto/high/low) → dispatch
Cuts frontier spend on every OTHER automation you run

Publish gate
Draft done → yes/no batch on quality checks → ship or review
Turns content pipelines from supervised to sampled

Scheduled sorters
Daily cron → classify the day’s pile → filed + flagged list
The compounding one — boring, weekly, forever

Computer-use tasks
Goal in → agent plans, Jev operates → sensitive actions stop for a human
The Jev-Desktop-for-Codex pattern — speed with a leash

Start with whichever row matches a decision you already make every week — boring-plus-recurring is the whole qualification. My own first two were exactly the video’s demos: Search Console keyword triage and inbox routing, both variants of rows one and five.

## Safeguards and the personalisation shortcut

Three safeguards separate durable jev automation from a week-two horror story. Confidence gates everywhere — non-negotiable. Human-in-the-loop on sensitive classes — the computer-use builds gate anything consequential to a person by design, and yours should too (payments, sends, deletes). And a “do nothing” option in every schema — the safety valve that lets the model decline instead of forcing a bad pick. None of these cost speed on the 95% that flows; they exist for the 5% that shouldn’t.

Boundary honesty: Jev automates JUDGEMENT between known options — it cannot write the email, explain its reasoning, or handle open-ended work; pair it with your writing models for those (the routing row does exactly that). top_items.content:
Wondering how to use the Claude Code send now key? The quick version is just below — it’s the ctrl+enter shortcut Anthropic shipped in v2.1.275 on 17 September 2026, and it fixes the single most annoying thing about steering long agent turns.

Short answer:

- Press Ctrl+Enter (or Ctrl+X, Ctrl+S) to interrupt the current turn and send every queued message at once.

- Shipped in Claude Code v2.1.275 on 17 September 2026, per the official changelog.

- Sent and queued messages now show in grey until the model actually receives them.

- The same release added skills and plugin syncing from your claude.ai account to terminal sessions.

- Biggest win: you can redirect a long-running agent without mashing Escape and losing your queued context.

## What the Claude Code send now key actually does

Straight from the official Claude Code changelog for v2.1.275 (17 September 2026): “Added a send-now key (ctrl+enter, or ctrl+x ctrl+s) that interrupts the current turn and sends all queued messages at once; sent and queued messages show in gray until the model receives them.”

If you’ve spent any real time in Claude Code, you already know why this matters. The old workflow had two bad options while Claude was mid-turn: queue messages and wait — sometimes minutes on a long agentic run — for the turn to finish before your steering input landed, or hit Escape to interrupt, which stops the work dead and forces you to re-prompt. The send now key is the missing third option: keep typing guidance as you think of it, then hit Ctrl+Enter the moment steering matters more than letting the current step finish.

The grey-text change is small but genuinely useful. Messages you’ve sent or queued render in grey until the model receives them, so you always know what Claude has actually seen versus what’s still waiting. No more guessing whether your correction made it into the turn.

## How to use the Claude Code send now key in real workflows

Here’s how I’ve been using it since the update, running content and SEO automations:

- Course-correct long agent runs: when Claude starts down the wrong path on step 2 of 10, queue the correction and Ctrl+Enter immediately. You lose the current step, not the whole run.

- Batch your steering: queue three or four small instructions while watching the output, then send them as one interruption instead of four separate ones. Fewer interruptions, less token churn — which pairs nicely with the tricks in my guide to reducing Claude Code token usage.

- Escalate only when needed: plain Enter still queues politely for the end of the turn. Ctrl+Enter is the “no, now” button. Knowing both exist changes how you type.

If you’re tuning the rest of your setup at the same time, the effort level setting and mouse support are the other two quality-of-life updates worth turning on this month.

OMH New Feature: Jev Skills

Six new skills bring Jev’s typed decision-making into Hermes workflows:

• omh-jev-ask
Ask yes/no, pick-one, or scored questions and get probabilities instead of prose.

• omh-jev-route
Use Jev to choose between workflows when OMH routing is uncertain.

• omh-jev-failure-triage
Decide whether to retry, fix a dependency, request access, or change the approach after a failure.

• omh-jev-review-gate
Flag authentication, test coverage, migration, and severity risks in code diffs.

• omh-jev-action-check
Screen risky commands for secret exposure, outbound actions, and blast radius before execution.

• omh-jev-done-check
Test completion claims against observed evidence and surface anything still missing.

Jev provides the probabilities. OMH applies the workflow rules. Execution, approval, and merge decisions remain under user control.

OMH: https://t.co/g1exHwWK5E
